newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico coffee roasters win robusta import approval.
newsitem.headline: Mexico coffee roasters win robusta import approval.

text.p: Mexican coffee roasters, struggling to get their hands on beans from the national crop, have persuaded the government to allow imports this year of 150,000 60-kg bags of robustas, coffee sources said Tuesday.

Ruben Castillo Fragaso, executive president of Mexican Coffee Council, told Reuters the council and the Trade and Agriculture ministries have approved the restricted amounts of tariff-free imports between July and September.
Exports from the national crop have flowed rapidly this cycle, spurred in part by attractive prices, and little coffee remains in the country until the new crop cycle starts in October.

Castillo, head of the government's umbrella group for the sector, said no specific import quotas had yet been applied to the agreed 150,000 bag amount and that no specific applications for import permits had been made.

"High coffee prices in international markets in recent weeks have led to the export of all types of Mexican coffees, given that exports are not controled, running the risk that during thye months of July to September, the roasting industry could suffer a shortage of supplies," Castillo said.
"To avoid this problem, it was considered necessary to open up the option of complementary imports of the commodity," Castillo added.
Castillo shot down reports that Mexico was to allow imports of arabica beans, stressing it was for robustas. He declined to name the roasters involved.
Coffee markets were shaken last week after reports swirled that Mexico was about to dip into the already-scarce arabica buyers market to top up internal supplies for domestic consumption.

Mexican exporters and traders shrugged off the reports as ludicrous because Mexico's major domestic consumption being soluble coffee, which is largely made up of mixing robustas and other low grade beans.
"There is no way any Mexican roaster is going to seek to import arabicas, the price is too high and that is what will make it prohibitive," one exporter told Reuters.

Francisco Gurria Trevino, director of the Agriculture Ministry's National Farming Health Commission, told the Reforma newspaper that he had no news about imports as yet. Gurria's is in charge of dispatching import permits.
Another exporter, who declined to be named, said he had heard that roasters were trying to come to an accord to share out the 150,000 bags before making official applications for permits.

Swiss-based Nestle, he said, was looking for the lion's share of the import allocation, given it is the market leader of soluble coffee in the country. Spokesmen for Nestle, which markets the Nescafe brand, were not immediately availble for comment.
National Coffee Industry Association, Mexico's roaster group, last week denied any knowledge of industrialists' plans to import beans.
General manager Jorge Cisneros acknowledged, however, that private roasters could be in talks with the government to come to an accord.
Mexico has had to turn to import robustas in the past. Only about 4 percent of the coffee grown in Mexico are robustas, the remaining 96 percent being arabica.
Considering the politically-sensitive nature of a major coffee producer having to import beans, imports in previous years have also had to be pacted with the government.
